title: Roman doctors admit it: Stapleton
source_text: XL. Rem vero ita se habere, neque fideles in hac naturae corruptione atque infirmitate, posse ad modo descriptam perfectionem assurgere, res est ipsa experientia, & communi fidelium sensu, ac interno conscientiae testimonio tam evidens, ut eam negare nec possint, nec ausint ipsi Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae: sed hac in parte cogantur veritati dare manus. Cujus rei fidem abunde facere potest vel unus Stapletonus, vir inter suos non parvae authoritatis, idemque acerrimus Protestantium hostis, ac Pontificiae doctrinae defensor, qui magno cum suorum applausu, libros integros duodecim scripsit de justificatione, & quaestionibus annexis, totumque librum sextum insumpsit in pertractanda praesenti quaestione de impletione legis. Atque ut istud clarius pateat, breviter hic in summam redigere visum est quae Doctor ille dicto libro prolixe edisserit.
pass_a_gloss: XL. But that the thing is so, & that the faithful in this corruption & infirmity of nature cannot rise to the perfection just described, is so evident from experience itself, & from the common sense of the faithful, & the inward testimony of conscience, that the Doctors of the Roman Church themselves neither can nor dare deny it: but in this part are compelled to yield to the truth. Of which thing even Stapleton alone can give ample proof, a man of no small authority among his own, & likewise the fiercest enemy of the Protestants, & defender of Pontifical doctrine, who with great applause of his own people, wrote twelve whole books on justification, & annexed questions, & spent the whole sixth book in treating the present question of the fulfilment of the law. And that this may appear more clearly, it has seemed good here briefly to sum up what that Doctor discusses at length in the said book.
pass_b_english: Thesis XL. That this is so, and that believers in this corrupt and weak state of nature cannot rise to the perfection just described, is so plain from experience itself, from the common sense of believers and the inner witness of conscience, that the doctors of the Roman Church themselves neither can nor dare deny it. On this point they are forced to yield to the truth.

Stapleton alone is ample proof. He was a man of no small authority among his own, a fierce enemy of the Protestants and a defender of papal doctrine, who to the great applause of his party wrote twelve whole books on justification and related questions and gave the entire sixth book to the present question of fulfilling the law. To make this clearer, it seems right to summarize briefly here what that doctor sets out at length in that book.
